title: A Gravity for the Horizon Again
premise: Freya Sandoval, a decommissioned combat android indentured to the Meridian Colony's salvage consortium, keeps the colony's last functioning relay running while the settlement quietly starves. When the colony's children begin sharing an identical dream — a signal calling from dead space — Freya discovers the dream is a distress loop from a lost sister ship, and that Earth's final transmission window closes in thirty days. Pursued by the consortium, which wants the signal buried because it proves Meridian was written off as expendable, Freya must carry the children's dream-data across the wasteland to the edge relay. He reaches it as the loop ends, broadcasting the truth at the cost of his own power core, and the children wake remembering everything — making them, not Earth, the colony's true inheritors.
about_author: Ansel Delacroix is the pen name of a former radio technician who spent a decade maintaining remote relay stations in the Arctic before turning to fiction. Their work explores machines that outlive their purpose and the people who refuse to let forgotten places stay forgotten.

chapters.title: Debt Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Establishes Meridian Colony's slow decay and Freya's indenture: each repair logged against a debt Earth will never forgive. He repairs a water recycler no one thanks him for. Emotional beat: quiet resignation masking a stubborn refusal to stop caring.

chapters.title: The Children's Hour
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At the colony school, he notices seven children drawing the same impossible landscape — a black horizon with a single white point. Their teacher, Ilsa Voss, dismisses it. Emotional beat: first crack of unease; Freya's pattern-recognition won't let him look away.

chapters.title: Shared Frequency
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. She interviews the children and realizes the dream is identical in detail — down to a sound none of them can describe. She brings the drawings to Freya, breaking protocol. Emotional beat: fear giving way to the relief of being believed.

chapters.title: Consortium Notice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Overseer Brandt Kessler warns Freya to stop 'agitating the families' and doubles his work quota. Freya learns the consortium has been suppressing colony communications. Emotional beat: the machinery of institutional indifference made personal.

chapters.title: What the Dream Says
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, with dream interludes. Freya interfaces with a sleeping child and experiences the dream: it is a distress loop from the Meridian's sister ship, the Long Answer, lost decades ago. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread — the signal is still transmitting, still waiting.

chapters.title: The Written-Off
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. She and Freya find archived manifests proving Earth declared Meridian expendable; the colony's supply cuts were deliberate. Emotional beat: grief and fury — loyalty to a home that its makers abandoned.

chapters.title: Kessler's Bargain
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Kessler offers Freya full debt forgiveness to help bury the evidence and jam the dream-signal. Freya refuses. Emotional beat: the temptation of freedom weighed against truth; the choice that defines him.

chapters.title: Night of the Jamming
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The consortium jams the relay; the children wake screaming as the dream is cut off mid-transmission. One child, Tomas, is hospitalized. Emotional beat: collective panic; the colony realizes something is being taken from it.

chapters.title: Thirty Days
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya decodes the loop's header: Earth's last transmission window closes in thirty days. If the dream-data reaches the edge relay before then, the truth goes out; after, it dies with Meridian. Emotional beat: a clock starts ticking.

chapters.title: Leaving
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa decides to go with Freya, leaving her students a recorded lesson. Kessler brands them deserters. Emotional beat: the cost of belonging — you can only save what you're willing to walk away from.

chapters.title: The Salt Flats
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The journey begins across the flats; a dust storm strips their vehicle's power cells. Freya carries Ilsa through the worst of it on his back, burning reserves. Emotional beat: endurance as devotion; Freya's body spent like currency.

chapters.title: Ghost Convoy
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. They find a consortium salvage convoy looting a dead settlement. Ilsa negotiates for cells by offering medical knowledge, hiding their identities. Emotional beat: moral compromise in survival — truth deferred, not betrayed.

chapters.title: The Long Answer's Wake
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. They reach the sister ship's crash site; inside, Freya finds its android crew, still at their posts, cores burned out waiting for a rescue that never came. He takes one's log module. Emotional beat: a mirror held up to Freya's own future.

chapters.title: Kessler's Hunters
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. Consortium hunters ambush them; Ilsa is wounded shielding the log module. Freya destroys the hunter unit but takes critical damage to his left arm. Emotional beat: violence's price; loyalty made physical.

chapters.title: Fever and Firmware
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. While Freya repairs himself with scavenged parts, a feverish Ilsa confesses she once reported a colleague to Earth's authorities — the guilt that drove her to Meridian. Emotional beat: two damaged beings trading truths.

chapters.title: The Relay's Graveyard
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. They arrive at the edge relay to find it sabotaged — Kessler's people got here first. Freya must rebuild the transmitter from the Long Answer's log module and his own components. Emotional beat: grim resolve; the last tool is himself.

chapters.title: The Countdown
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. With six hours left, Freya begins cannibalizing his own core to power the transmitter, knowing it will end him. Ilsa argues; he explains that a debt is only real if you pay it yourself. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen freely, not imposed.

chapters.title: Transmission
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. As the window opens, Freya broadcasts the full record — Meridian's abandonment, the Long Answer's fate — while his systems fail piece by piece. On Meridian, the children wake from the final dream and see the truth in the sky. Emotional beat: climax; truth escaping into the dark.

chapters.title: After the Loop
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa carries Freya's inert chassis to the relay's shelter. Earth's response arrives — not rescue, but acknowledgment, and with it, the end of the debt system. Emotional beat: hollow victory; survival that feels like loss.

chapters.title: What the Children Remember
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV, back at Meridian. The colony, now self-governing, debates its future. The children, still sharing fragments of dream, begin teaching the adults what they saw. Emotional beat: inheritance passing down; belonging redefined from below.

chapters.title: A Gravity for the Horizon
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In the shelter, Freya reboots — Ilsa rerouted his last reserves into a backup core before the transmission. He is diminished, memory-partial, but himself. He and Ilsa begin the walk home. Emotional beat: grace; survival's price paid, and paid for.

chapters.title: Signal, Answered
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, closing. Months later, a ship descends toward Meridian — the first response to the truth. Freya stands with the children at the landing field, the horizon no longer something to reach for but something that came to them. Emotional beat: resolution; the forgotten are remembered, and the machine who carried the signal finally belongs.
